[01]{.num} [Kick-off]{.kicker}

## A loaf of bread

At its heart, the gambling industry is just like most others: it sells something for a different price than it's actually worth.

Think about a loaf of bread in the shop. You might think *"I could make that cheaper myself"*, and you'd probably be right. The shop's price includes flour, ovens, staff, rent… and a bit of profit on top.

Bets work exactly the same way. The bookmaker, sportsbook or casino (let's just call it **the house**) has costs to cover and expects a profit. It gets both by **paying out winning bets at a little less than their true price**.
:::


::: {.pullquote}
Bookmakers think in probabilities.<br>Players think in odds.
:::

::: {.band .sea}
[02]{.num} [Half-time]{.kicker}

## Two languages, one idea

To set a fair price, the house first uses **probability theory** to work out how likely something is to happen. Then it adjusts that number to include its profit margin.

Players, meanwhile, don't care much about probability. They want to know **how much they could win**. That's what odds tell them.

The lovely part? The two are connected by one of the simplest formulas in all of maths:

::: {.formula}
decimal odds = **1 ÷ probability**
:::

::: {.odds-table}
| Chance of happening | Probability | Fair decimal odds | You get back from €10 |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Coin lands heads | 50% | 2.00 | €20 |
| One suit from a deck | 25% | 4.00 | €40 |
| Rolling a six | 16.7% | 6.00 | €60 |
:::
:::

::: {.band .coral}
[03]{.num} [Full-time]{.kicker}

## Where the profit hides

Take a fair coin. Heads and tails are 50/50, so the **fair odds** are 2.00 on each side. But the house doesn't offer 2.00. It offers **1.90**.

::: {.odds-table .coin-table}
| Selection | Fair / true chance | Fair / true odds | House odds offered |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Heads | 50% | 2.00 | 1.90 |
| Tails | 50% | 2.00 | 1.90 |
:::

Turn the house's odds back into probabilities (1 ÷ 1.90) and each side becomes **52.6%**, so the book adds up to **105.3%**. A coin can't have a 105.3% chance of landing on something: that extra **5.3%** is the house's margin, known in the trade as the **overround**.

Flip it round and you get the **return to player (RTP)**: 1 ÷ 1.053 ≈ **95%**. For every €100 bet, about **€95 comes back** to players and **€5 stays with the house**.

On any single flip, anything can happen. But over many flips and many bets, the results drift towards the maths, and **the maths is on the house's side**.

**And that, in a nutshell, is how the gambling industry works:** offer slightly lower odds than the true chance deserves, and let the long run do the rest.
:::
